newsitem.title: FRANCE: French deputies slam Britain over mad cow crisis.
newsitem.headline: French deputies slam Britain over mad cow crisis.

text.p: A French parliamentary commission on Tuesday blasted Britain for hiding the full facts about mad cow disease and accused London of trying to blackmail its neighbours in the 10-month-old beef crisis.

A six-month inquiry set up by the National Assembly (lower house) found "intolerable" lapses in Britain's handling of the affair, inadequate controls by the European Union and a lack of coordination in France, a report issued on Tuesday showed.

The report's author, French deputy Jean-Francois Mattei, said there was no question of quickly lifting the embargo on British beef, imposed after the crisis over mad cow disease, or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), erupted last March.
"French politicians are not ready to accept an end to the embargo on British meat," he told journalists at a briefing on the findings. "This situation is a necessary one," he said.

The 200-page document, together with nearly 700 pages of evidence given to a special parliamentary committee, is the most detailed French investigation so far into the disease which has ravaged British herds and spread consumer panic across Europe.
Reviving a row over Britain's "non-cooperation" tactics in trying to get the ban lifted, the report said London had shown neither cooperation nor a sense of its partners' interests.
"It is unacceptable that political blackmail can be used by one member to block collective decisions taken in a community linked together by solidarity," it said.

British Prime Minister John Major adopted a policy of non-cooperation, blocking some EU business in Brussels, for several weeks to show his frustration before EU leaders agreed a compromise on lifting the ban at a Florence summit last June.
So far the European Union says conditions agreed then for a gradual lifting of the global export ban have not been met.

The French report also heaped blame on Britain for failing to pass on all the results of its research into mad cow disease, although it also said the progress of British research may have discouraged French scientists from speeding up their own work.
Scientists are looking for further proof of a suspected link between BSE and a fatal human brain disorder, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), which triggered the public scare over beef.
